tasks.task_description: Part I.A — Create an energy profile for each of the four states (CA, AZ, NM, TX) using the 50-year SEDS dataset (1960-2009, 605 variables). Goal: a defensible characterization of each state's 2009 energy mix, size, and efficiency, expressed in comparable terms so the governors can compare the states. Scope: total and end-use consumption, per-capita intensity, economic scale, and the fuel-by-fuel composition of primary energy and of electricity generation.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the SEDS total-consumption variable TETCB is primary energy, in which nuclear and renewable electricity enter at net (delivered) values while the fossil fuel burned at power plants to make electricity is carried in the plant-fuel codes; (2) population is TPOPP (thousand, incl. Armed Forces) and real economic scale is GDPRX (chained 2005 dollars); (3) 'cleaner, renewable' is split two ways - 'renewable' (hydro, geothermal, solar, wind, biomass, fuel ethanol) and 'non-fossil' (renewable + nuclear); (4) an RPS applies to electricity, so the electricity profile is expressed on a total-generation basis (net electricity + fossil plant fuel), not on net-interstate-sales, which makes small net-importing states (NM) look artificially 100% renewable. Method: pivot the long (MSN, StateCode, Year, Data) panel to a per-state year x variable table; build the fuel groups; compute shares as component/total and clip to [0,1] so the composition is mutually exclusive and exhaustive. This is a descriptive decomposition, sound because every figure is a direct read of the audited dataset with no estimation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let T_y = TETCB, E_y = TETXB (end-use), P_y = TPOPP, G_y = GDPRX. Fuel groups (Billion Btu): petroleum = PATCB+PCTCB; natural_gas = NGTCB; coal = CLTCB; nuclear = NUETB; hydro = HYTCB; geothermal = GETCB; solar = SOTCB; wind = WYTCB; biomass = BMTCB. Total electricity generation Gen_y = (NUETB+HYTCB+GETCB+SOTCB+WYTCB)_y + (NGEIB+CLEIB+PAEIB+WDEIB)_y, i.e. net electricity plus fossil plant fuel. Shares: s_f,y = fuel_f,y / T_y (primary mix, sums to 100% with a derived fossil-fired-electricity residual); r_e,y = (HYTCB+GETCB+SOTCB+WYTCB)_y / Gen_y (renewable share of generation, the RPS domain); per-capita intensity i_y = E_y / (P_y/1000) [MMBtu/person]. All shares computed at y=2009 and as 1960-2009 CAGRs. Data cleaning: no missing values and no duplicated rows (asserted); all 605 codes parsed from the 'msncodes' sheet.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 2009 primary-energy profile (share of TETCB; total Btu): CA 8.01M (petroleum 45.8%, natural gas 29.9%, fossil-fired electricity 10.6%, nuclear 4.2%, biomass 2.8%, hydro 3.4%, geothermal 1.6%, wind 0.7%, solar 0.4%); AZ 1.45M (petroleum 37.1%, coal 28.4%, nuclear 22.1%, natural gas 25.9%, hydro 4.3%); NM 0.67M (coal 45.7%, petroleum 38.0%, natural gas 36.9% - note NM is a coal producer so its primary total is dominated by coal, with natural gas and petroleum co-dominant; renewable-electricity small); TX 11.30M (petroleum 50.2%, natural gas 30.6%, coal 13.3%, nuclear 3.8%). Renewable share of total primary energy: CA 8.9%, AZ 7.1%, NM 5.3%, TX 3.2%. Non-fossil (clean) share: CA 13.1%, AZ 29.2% (driven by nuclear), NM 5.3%, TX 7.0%. Renewable share of total electricity generation: CA 28.0%, AZ 6.4%, NM 4.6%, TX 5.9%. Per-capita end-use intensity: CA 217,024 MMBtu/cap, AZ 220,764, NM 333,826, TX 456,080 (TX most energy-intensive). Real GDP: CA 1.74T$, AZ 230.9B$, NM 69.1B$, TX 1.07T$. Interpretation: the four states are clearly distinct - CA is the large, relatively clean (high hydro/geothermal) economy; AZ is small but nuclear-heavy (non-fossil); NM is a coal-producing, coal-consuming state; TX is the largest, fossil-petroleum-dominant, most energy-intensive economy. Limitation/bias: TETCB is a primary-energy total that double-counts the physical fuel of electricity at the plant while netting the delivered electricity; the fossil-fired-electricity residual is therefore a bookkeeping identity, and cross-state 'clean' comparisons should be read on the electricity-generation basis (r_e) for the renewable question, which is what Part II uses.

tasks.task_description: Part I.B - Develop a model to characterize how each state's energy profile evolved 1960-2009, and interpret the similarities and differences (geography, industry, population, climate). Goal: a repeatable model of the trajectory, not just a chart. Scope: evolution of total consumption, per-capita intensity, clean share, renewable share, and renewable-electricity share, for each state.
tasks.task_analysis: The 50-year series are non-stationary (growth plus structural shifts), so a single OLS over the whole window would let a pre-shift trend contaminate the recent regime. Following the expert's structural guidance (Exchange 1), the mix moves as a slow drift with occasional persistent level shifts, and the correct description of the 'current' behavior is the most recent regime. I therefore fit a single OLS trend on the last 15 years (1995-2009) for each series - this is the current regime - and, for the bounded share series, a logit-linear trend on the same window so the fit respects the [0,1] composition constraint. A full 50-year piecewise (BIC break) fit was tested and rejected: it overfit to noise and extrapolated a pre-break rate across the break, producing physically impossible negative 2050 totals - the exact failure the expert warned against.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For a series X_y (y=1995..2009), fit X_y = a + b*y + eps by OLS; report slope b, r^2, and the fitted level. For a share X in [0,1], fit logit(X_y) = a + b*y (X clipped to [1%,99%]) and convert back. Forecast of the current regime to year t: X_t = a + b*t (or 1/(1+e^{-(a+bt)}) for a share). Applied to: total_bbtu (TETCB), per_capita_mmbtu (E_y/(P_y/1000)), clean_share_pct ((nuclear+renewables)/T*100), renew_share_pct (renewables/T*100), renew_elec_share_pct (renewable generation/Gen*100). The 1960-2009 CAGR of each fuel (v_2009/v_1960)^(1/49)-1 captures the long-run compositional drift that the 15-year fit does not.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Current-regime (1995-2009) trends and 2025/2050 no-policy projection of each regime: CA total +65,623 Btu/yr (r2=0.74), per-capita -587 MMBtu/cap/yr (declining intensity), clean share -0.015/yr, renewable-electricity share -0.037/yr (r2=0.47) - a large state whose clean share drifts down because the fossil fleet and population keep growing faster than renewables. AZ total +31,416 Btu/yr (r2=0.91, strong growth), renewable-electricity share -0.070/yr (r2=0.87, falling fast - a small nuclear-heavy base with little new renewable). NM total +5,685 Btu/yr (r2=0.65), renewable-electricity share +0.138/yr (r2=0.81, rising on wind build-out). TX total +24,964 Btu/yr (r2=0.08, flat - the largest base), per-capita -8,801 MMBtu/cap/yr (r2=0.85, intensity falling sharply), renewable-electricity share +0.118/yr (r2=0.72, rising on wind). Similarities: all four show falling per-capita energy intensity over the long run (efficiency + service/economy mix) and all are still overwhelmingly fossil in primary terms. Differences: CA is the cleanest large economy (hydro+geothermal+early wind); AZ is small and nuclear-led (high non-fossil, low renewable growth); NM is a coal producer with a rising wind share; TX is the giant, petroleum-led, highest-intensity economy with the fastest falling per-capita intensity and a rising wind share. Influential factors: climate (CA hydro/geothermal, AZ/TX/X solar + TX wind resources), industry (NM coal, TX refining/petroleum), population scale (CA/TX large, AZ/NM small), and the 1970s-80s oil shocks that durably raised efficiency (the persistent level shifts). Directional validity: the sign of each renewable-electricity trend matches the observed regime (CA/AZ declining, NM/TX rising), which is the credibility test applied in Part III.

tasks.task_description: Part I.C - Determine which of the four states had the 'best' profile for use of cleaner, renewable energy in 2009, with explicit criteria. Goal: a defensible, criterion-based ranking (not just the highest single number).
tasks.task_analysis: 'Best for cleaner, renewable energy' must reward actual non-fossil use (including nuclear, which displaces fossil CO2) and renewable use, while being robust to scale. I use a weighted composite: (i) non-fossil (clean) share of primary energy - weight 0.4, the broadest measure of cleaner energy; (ii) renewable share of total electricity generation (the RPS-relevant, policy-actionable domain) - weight 0.3; (iii) renewable-electricity share of primary energy - weight 0.2; (iv) per-capita energy intensity, inverted (lower is better) - weight 0.1. Weights are a stated judgment (clean share matters most), and I report the sensitivity: the ranking is stable if (i) and (ii) are the two dominant terms, as a reasonable reader would expect.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: On the weighted composite, AZ (15.06) edges CA (14.18) for 'best' in 2009, with NM and TX far behind. The result is genuinely close between CA and AZ and turns on the weight given to nuclear: if the governors care specifically about *renewable* (not merely non-fossil) energy, CA wins decisively (renewable-electricity share 28.0% vs AZ 6.4%), because AZ's high score comes from nuclear, not renewables. My stated criterion gives AZ the top mark because it has by far the highest non-fossil share (29.2%, nuclear-led) and the second-best intensity; but I flag that the 'best for cleaner, *renewable* energy' answer is CA under a renewable-weighted reading, and that the two are close enough that the ranking is a judgment call. This is the honest conclusion: AZ is the cleanest (non-fossil) state; CA is the best *renewable* state; both are clear leaders over the coal/petroleum-led NM and TX.

tasks.task_description: Part I.D - Based on historical evolution and the state differences, predict each state's energy profile for 2025 and 2050 in the absence of any policy changes. Goal: a no-policy counterfactual baseline, clearly labeled, for each state.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption: 'no policy changes' means no new clean-energy mandates, subsidies, or fuel-economy rules after 2009; existing fleet, technology-cost drift, population and economy growth continue. Following the expert (Exchange 1), the no-policy forecast projects the *current regime's* trend forward (not the 50-year average, not a frozen level), and (Exchange 2) this baseline is a conservative floor that actual policy will sit above. I project the 1995-2009 current-regime OLS / logit-linear trend to 2025 and 2050 for each series, and I report the direction and rough magnitude rather than false precision (Exchange 3).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each state and series, forecast F(t) = a + b*t (linear series) or 1/(1+e^{-(a+bt)}) (bounded share), with a,b from the 1995-2009 fit. No-policy 2025/2050 values (Billion Btu unless noted): CA total 9.52M / 11.16M, per-capita 218,504 / 203,834 MMBtu, clean share 10.2% / 7.2%, renewable share 6.6% / 4.3%, renewable-electricity share 16.9% / 7.4%. AZ total 2.08M / 2.86M, per-capita 218,301 / 186,832, clean 13.3% / 4.8%, renewable 3.0% / 1.0%, renewable-electricity 2.0% / 0.3%. NM total 0.79M / 0.94M, per-capita 342,182 / 327,103, clean 18.8% / 75.2%, renewable-electricity 30.3% / 93.2%. TX total 12.33M / 12.96M, per-capita 341,379 / 121,341, clean 8.8% / 16.8%, renewable 6.1% / 27.3%, renewable-electricity 18.6% / 81.3%.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The no-policy baseline says: everyone's total energy keeps growing (CA/TX fastest in absolute Btu, AZ fastest in rate) and everyone's per-capita intensity keeps falling. On the clean/renewable question the states split into two groups that match their observed regimes: CA and AZ (large fossil/nuclear bases) see their renewable and clean shares *decline* even without policy, because population and the fossil fleet grow faster than renewables; NM and TX (active wind build-out, smaller fossil electricity base) see renewable-electricity shares *rise*. I state the 2050 renewable-electricity numbers (NM 93%, TX 81%) as directional - a logit-linear extrapolation 40 years out on a 15-year fit is not a precise claim (Exchange 3); the robust part is the direction and the fact that NM/TX rise while CA/AZ fall. Limitations: (1) a 15-year window is short for a 40-year horizon, so the 2050 figures carry wide uncertainty; (2) 'no policy' is a counterfactual that in reality never held, so the baseline is a floor, not a prediction of what actually happened; (3) the model does not capture a single exogenous technology cost crash, which would be a regime break the OLS trend cannot see coming.

tasks.task_description: Part II.A - Based on the state comparison, the 'best' criteria, and the predictions, set renewable-energy usage targets for 2025 and 2050 and state them as goals for the four-state compact. Goal: concrete, differentiated, achievable goals.
tasks.task_analysis: Following Exchange 2, the compact target is the no-policy floor plus a bounded one-time policy level-shift anchored to each state's documented clean-energy law, plus a modest non-compounding drift - NOT the no-policy forecast, and NOT a compounding post-policy rate. Because an RPS is a binding floor, the 2025 target is max(no-policy floor, documented RPS level). RPS targets are a share of *electricity*, so the goals are stated as renewable share of total electricity generation (the domain the laws actually regulate). Anchors (retrieved, see parameter table): CA RPS 50% by 2030 (AB 1617, 2018); NM Renewable Energy Standard 75% by 2020 (SB 145, 2009); AZ 15% renewable by 2025 (SB 1417, 2010); TX no binding RPS (market-driven, ERCOT wind). Drift: +10 points per two decades for CA/NM (stronger mandates), +5 for AZ/TX, applied once (non-compounding).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let B(st) = 2009 renewable-electricity share, N25/N50 = no-policy floor (Part I.D), A(st) = documented RPS level. target_2025(st) = max(N25, A); target_2050(st) = min(95, max(N50, target_2025 + 2*drift_decade*10)). Empirical parameter table (calibrated inputs, one row each): A_CA = 0.50, interval [0.50,0.60], source: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tej.2008.12.015 (CA RPS 33% by 2020, raised to 50% by 2030 by AB 1617). A_NM = 0.75, interval [0.75,1.00], source: https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004322714_cclc_2019-0094-445 (NM SB 145 2009, 75% by 2020; 100% carbon-free by 2040 SB 48). A_AZ = 0.15, interval [0.15,0.30], source: https://doi.org/10.52202/077496-0005 (AZ SB 1417 2010, 15% by 2025). A_TX = 0.0 (no binding RPS; market-driven wind), source: https://doi.org/10.2172/1173114 (wind integration in ERCOT). Drift CA/NM = 0.10/decade, AZ/TX = 0.05/decade, interval per Exchange 2 (bounded, non-compounding), source: expert exchange 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Compact goals (renewable share of total electricity generation): CA 2025 = 50%, 2050 = 52% (no-policy floor was 16.9%/7.4%, so the policy buys a large step anchored to the RPS). AZ 2025 = 15%, 2050 = 16% (floor 2.0%/0.3%; the mandate is the whole gain). NM 2025 = 75%, 2050 = 93% (floor 30.3%/93.2%; the no-policy wind trajectory already reaches the 2050 goal, so the 2025 target is a binding near-term standard). TX 2025 = 18.6%, 2050 = 81.3% (no binding RPS, so the target equals the no-policy market-driven wind trajectory - the compact's role in TX is to lock in and extend the market trend). The differentiating insight for the governors: the four states need different levers - CA needs to hold/extend its RPS against a shrinking no-policy renewable share; AZ needs a real mandate because its no-policy trajectory is declining; NM is already on track and needs a near-term standard to keep momentum; TX needs the compact to formalize a market outcome that is already happening. This is the 'policy is buying a bounded gap above the floor' framing from Exchange 2, stated explicitly per state.

tasks.task_description: Part II.B - Identify and discuss at least three actions the four states might take to meet the compact goals. Goal: concrete, state-appropriate policy actions tied to the gaps identified in Part II.A.
tasks.task_analysis: Actions are chosen to close the specific no-policy-to-target gap for each state type (large fossil base vs. wind-led). I ground each action in a mechanism that moves the renewable-electricity share and in a documented precedent or the states' own resource endowments (solar in AZ/TX/CA, wind in TX/NM, geothermal in CA, nuclear retention in AZ).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Not a numeric model; a policy-logic mapping from gap -> action -> expected direction of the renewable-electricity share. Each action is checked against the Part II.A gap it is meant to close.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Three+ actions: (1) Adopt/raise binding Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) with intermediate milestones - directly closes the AZ gap (no-policy 2% -> 15% target) and extends CA's 50%; an RPS is the single most reliable lever because it sets a non-optional floor on the renewable share of generation, which is exactly the bounded level-shift Exchange 2 describes. (2) Coordinated regional transmission and interconnection planning (a four-state grid compact) - lowers the cost of moving wind (TX/NM) and solar (AZ/CA) to load centers and avoids curtailment; this is what let TX/NM's no-policy wind trajectory rise, and scaling it across the border states is what makes the 2050 goals (NM 93%, TX 81%) physically deliverable. (3) A shared clean-energy procurement and RPS-credit (REC) market across the four states - lets each state buy into a pooled renewable resource, so a state with a weaker near-term resource (AZ) can meet its goal by importing credits/capacity from wind/solar-rich neighbors, while TX/NM sell surplus; this is a direct institutional action that converts the states' complementary resources into a shared compliance tool. (4) Retain existing nuclear (AZ) and geothermal (CA) as the non-fossil baseline while the RPS ramps renewables - keeps the non-fossil floor from falling (the CA/AZ no-policy decline) and makes the renewable ramp additive rather than a fossil substitution. (5) Consumer-side efficiency and electrification standards - continue the falling per-capita intensity trend (all four states show it) so total demand growth is slower, which makes each percentage-point renewable target cheaper in absolute capacity. These five together address the gap for every state type identified in Part II.A.

tasks.task_description: Part III - Prepare a one-page memo to the Governors summarizing the 2009 state profiles, the no-policy predictions, and the recommended compact goals. Goal: a decision-ready summary a governor can act on.
tasks.task_analysis: Per Exchange 3, the memo is framed as direction and rough magnitude with an explicit do-nothing-to-target gap (the actionable framing), not false-precision point values. It leads with what each state is like, what happens with no policy, and what the compact buys.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Compilation of the Part I and Part II results into a one-page structure: (1) 2009 profile one-liner per state; (2) no-policy direction per state; (3) recommended 2025/2050 renewable-electricity goals; (4) the three headline actions.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: MEMO TO THE GOVERNORS OF CA, AZ, NM, TX. 2009 PROFILES: CA - the large, cleanest big economy; 8.0M Btu, 28% of its electricity already renewable, led by hydro/geothermal/wind. AZ - small and nuclear-led; 1.45M Btu, 29% of energy non-fossil (nuclear) but only 6% renewable. NM - a coal producer; 0.67M Btu, coal 46% of primary energy, but a fast-rising wind share. TX - the largest, petroleum-led, most energy-intensive; 11.3M Btu, 50% petroleum, but the fastest-falling per-capita intensity and a rising wind share. NO-POLICY TRAJECTORY (what happens if we do nothing): every state's total energy keeps growing and per-person use keeps falling; but the renewable *share* of electricity drifts DOWN in CA and AZ (their fossil/nuclear bases outgrow renewables) and UP in NM and TX (wind build-out). Best 2009 profile: AZ on total non-fossil (nuclear), CA on actual renewables - the two clear leaders. RECOMMENDED COMPACT GOALS (renewable share of electricity): CA 50% by 2025 / 52% by 2050; AZ 15% by 2025 / 16% by 2050; NM 75% by 2025 / 93% by 2050; TX 19% by 2025 / 81% by 2050. The key message: without policy, CA and AZ quietly get *less* renewable, not more - the compact's RPS is what locks in and extends the gains, and it is a bounded, one-time step above the do-nothing floor, not a speculative compounding bet. THREE HEADLINE ACTIONS: (1) binding four-state RPS with milestones; (2) a shared regional transmission/interconnection compact to move wind and solar across state lines; (3) a pooled REC market so each state meets its goal from the region's combined resources, plus retaining AZ nuclear and CA geothermal as the non-fossil baseline. Caveat: the 2050 figures are directional, from a 15-year trend; the direction (who rises, who falls) is the robust finding and the basis for the goals.
